rows.text: Strongly recommended: There is strong evidence and/or general consensus that the intervention or treatment is beneficial, useful, and effective.
Recommended: There is evidence and/or consensus that the intervention or treatment is beneficial, useful, and effective; the strength of the recommendation is weaker than Category I.
Weakly recommended: There is less evidence and/or consensus, but the intervention or treatment may still be considered beneficial, useful, and effective.
Not recommended: There is evidence and/or general consensus that the intervention or treatment is not beneficial, and in some cases, may be harmful.

• Smoking or exposure to secondhand smoke

• Impaired glucose tolerance (fasting plasma glucose 6.1-7.0 mmol/L and/or 2-hour postprandial glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L) or diabetes (fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L and/or 2-hour postprandial glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L)
• Dyslipidemia (total cholesterol ≥ 5.2 mmol/L or LDL-C ≥ 3.4 mmol/L or HDL-C < 1.0 mmol/L)
• Family history of early-onset cardiovascular disease (first-degree male relative < 55 years; first-degree female relative < 65 years)
• Abdominal obesity (waist circumference: Men ≥ 90 cm, Women ≥ 85 cm) or obesity (BMI ≥ 28 kg/m²)
• Increased heart rate (resting heart rate ≥ 80 beats per minute)
• Hyperuricemia (serum uric acid: men ≥ 420 μmol/L, women ≥ 360 μmol/L)
• LVH: Sokolow-Lyon voltage (SV1 + RV5/RV6) > 3.8 mV, Cornell voltage-duration product > 244 mV•ms, or echocardiographic LVMI ≥ 109 g/m² for men and ≥ 105 g/m² for women
• Carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) ≥ 0.9 mm or presence of carotid plaques

• eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73 m² or mild increase in serum creatinine levels (Men: 115-133 μmol/L, Women: 107-124 μmol/L) or microalbuminuria (urinary albumin excretion rate 30-300 mg/24 h, or urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) 30-300 mg/g)
• Heart disease: Myocardial infarction, angina, coronary revascularization, heart failure
• Kidney disease: Diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephropathy, renal insufficiency (including eGFR < 30 mL/min per 1.73 m² or proteinuria > 300 mg/24 h)
• Retinopathy: Hypertensive retinopathy with hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema
UNaspot represents spot urine sodium; UCrspot represents spot urine creatinine.

In hypertensive patients, the DASH diet can reduce systolic blood pressure by 11.4 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure
by 5.5 mmHg. Persistent adherence to the DASH diet can effectively lower the risk of cardiovascular events and all-
cause mortality.

In hypertensive patients, the CHH diet can reduce systolic blood pressure by 10 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure
by 3.8 mmHg. Researchers believe that adherence to the CHH diet could reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular diseases by 20%, heart failure by 28%, and all-cause mortality by 13%.

Among women, those who consume spicy foods more than three times per week have a 12% lower risk of hypertension compared to those who never eat spicy foods. The more frequently spicy foods are consumed, the more pronounced the reduction in systolic and diastolic blood pressure. In individuals who do not consume alcohol, the risk of hypertension is 28% lower in those who eat spicy foods daily compared to those who never eat them. Those who
prefer spicy foods consume 2.5 g less salt per day, and their systolic and diastolic blood pressures are 6.6 mmHg and 4.0 mmHg lower, respectively, than those who do not prefer spicy foods.
DASH diet: dietary approaches to stop hypertension; CHH diet: Chinese heart-healthy diet.
• Regular monitoring of weight changes is an important measure for preventing obesity.
• Ideally, total weight gain after adulthood should be controlled within 5 kg.
• For individuals who are already overweight or obese, it is necessary to control further weight gain or reduce weight.
• A balanced diet is key to weight management. Refer to section 5.2.1.2 for more details.
• The core of the diet should be diversity in food intake and maintaining a balanced diet while controlling total energy intake.
• For individuals who are already overweight or obese, reduce total energy intake by 500 to 1,000 kcal/day or by one-third of the recommended intake on the basis of a balanced diet.
• Control the intake of high-energy foods (such as high-fat foods, sugary drinks, and alcohol), and moderately limit the intake of carbohydrates.

• When implementing energy-restricted dietary interventions, especially very low-calorie diets, it is important to supplement with multivitamins and trace elements to prevent nutritional deficiencies caused by dietary restrictions.
Increase in Physical Activity and Exercise
• Appropriate physical activity is an important part of weight management. For increasing exercise, refer to section 5.2.1.6.
• Behavioral therapy, such as establishing awareness of dieting, developing meal plans, recording the types and amounts of food consumed, and calculating calories, can help with weight reduction.
Exercise Forms: Moderate-intensity continuous exercises such as walking, brisk walking, jogging, cycling, swimming, and HIIT.
Exercise Intensity: Moderate intensity (40%-60% of heart rate reserve); patients with lower cardiovascular risk may increase intensity to 60%-80% of heart rate reserve, or engage in HIIT.
Exercise Duration and Frequency: At least 10 minutes of continuous exercise per session, a minimum of 30 minutes per day, 5-7 days per week.
Target Muscles: Primarily the large muscles of the limbs and trunk-supporting muscles.
- Dynamic Resistance Exercise: Seated or standing arm raises, standing heel raises (lifting heels).
- Static Resistance Exercise: Seated or standing lateral arm raises; weighted lateral arm raises; wall-sit at a high position.

Exercise Intensity: For dynamic resistance exercises, use 50%-70% of 1RM*; for static or isometric resistance training, typically use low intensity (< 40% of 1RM) with intermittent grip strength exercises.

Exercise Duration and Frequency: For dynamic resistance exercises, repeat 8-12 times per set, progressively increasing to 2-3 sets per session, 2-3 times per week; for static or isometric resistance exercises, each session should last 2 minutes, with a total exercise duration of 12-15 minutes.
Target Muscles: Active expiratory and inspiratory muscles.

Exercise Forms: Awareness of cervical breathing, chest breathing, abdominal breathing, and the full process of exhalation and inhalation. Rhythmic breathing during aerobic exercise, with patterns such as one inhale followed by one exhale, or one inhale followed by three exhales. During resistance training, avoid holding your breath; synchronize breathing with slow movements, inhaling when exerting force and exhaling slowly during relaxation.
Exercise Intensity: Start breathing practice at 30%-50% of maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures.

Exercise Duration and Frequency: Relax and focus on breathing anytime and anywhere, consciously slow down or mentally count breaths, take a few deep breaths, with slow inhalations and even slower deep exhalations. Avoid hyperventilation caused by excessively rapid breathing.

Exercise Forms: Awareness of the neutral spine position, and gentle stretching that matches individual spinal joint mobility, including flexion, extension, lateral bending, and rotation of the cervical and thoracic spine. Gradual active stretching within the pain-free range of motion for the limbs; avoid forceful passive stretching with assistance. Synchronize breathing with specific stretching movements and avoid holding your breath during stretches.

HIIT: high-intensity interval training; *RM (Repetition Maximum): the maximum weight that can be lifted for one repetition, often understood
as the maximum number of repetitions possible.
